title: LeRoy vs East Rochester score, updates from Section V girls volleyball title game - Democrat and Chronicle
content: BLOOMFIELD – Only one team will hold the coveted sectional championship block. No. 1 LeRoy and No. 2 East Rochester will soon battle for the 2026 Section V Class C1 girls volleyball title. The winner will play Section V’s C2 champion for a spot in the state tournament. LeRoy seeks its third consecutive sectional crown in a rematch of a 2025 Class C1 semifinal which spanned five sets. LeRoy won set five, 15-12, to complete a 3-2 victory over East Rochester and win the 2026 Section V Class C1 girls volleyball championships. Shea Williams provided the final kill for the Oatkan Knights. LeRoy leads East Rochester, 10-7, in the fifth set of the Section V Class C1 girls volleyball final. East Rochester, needing a win in set four to extend its season, opened an 11-6 lead over LeRoy. LeRoy outlasted East Rochester, 25-20, to win the third set and take a 2-1 lead in the Class C1 final. Shea Williams' outside attacking and Harper Holly's play at the net have fueled LeRoy so far. Set two between East Rochester and LeRoy proved tighter than the first. East Rochester pulled away late to win, 25-21, and even the Class C1 final at one set apiece. LeRoy and East Rochester traded blows through half of the first set. The Oatkan Knights, however, pulled away once each side reached a dozen points. title: Why we describe elections as red v. blue—and why Mass. was different for decades - WCVB
content: Will this election be a blue wave for the Democrats, or will the red wall protect the Republicans' control of Congress? Where did the shorthand associating colors with the political parties come from in the first place? According to Smithsonian Magazine, it wasn’t until 1976 that the association of colors with political parties began. In the election between Republican incumbent Gerald Ford and Democratic challenger Jimmy Carter, blue was assigned to Ford, and red was assigned to Carter. “The notion that there were ‘red states’ and ‘blue states’ — and that the former were Republican and the latter Democratic — wasn’t cemented on the national psyche until the year 2000,” the magazine wrote. In Massachusetts, until this year, the colors in primary elections were actually reversed from that national stereotype, with Democrats in red and Republicans in blue. That was because the color system in Massachusetts predated the Ford-Carter election. The primary ballot colors were changed this year, but if Bay State voters approve Ballot Question 3 in this election, the September 2026 primary election could be the last in Massachusetts to be divided by political party. title: Toyota RAV4 Rebound Officially Not Enough To Beat Honda CR-V's SUV Dominance - CarBuzz
content: After nearly a year of its worst sales figures in a decade, Toyota is finally building enough RAV4s to match last year's demand. But it's still not enough, because we're about to see the industry crown a new best-selling SUV for the first time since 2017. The best month ever for the RAV4 hybrid and PHEV still isn't enough to close the gap on Honda's hottest seller, which is having an amazing year. Since 2017, the Toyota RAV4 has been the best-selling vehicle in the US that isn't a full-size pickup. It's not exactly the kind of thing you hang a banner in the rafters for, but for Toyota, selling close to 500,000 units in each of the last two years, is a big deal. But the Japanese automaker has been extremely slow to get the newest-generation RAV4 into full production, and sales have suffered. In the first half of the year, the RAV4 was down 35%. Now it's finally above where it was this month a year ago, with Toyota posting 39,888 sales in October for a threadbare increase of 0.6%. It's still down 26.2% for the year though, with sales at 293,552 versus 397,797 at the end of last October. But it shows customers still want a RAV when they can get it. Meanwhile at Honda, things have been going flat-out and it hasn't stopped. The company reported 34,815 CR-V sales last month, a new October record. That's not as many RAV4s as Toyota sold, but it's still a 9.8% increase for Honda's beloved SUV compared to last year. A deeper dive into the numbers shows some interesting trends. For the year so far, Honda has moved 371,659 CR-Vs, up 9.6% over the first 10 months of last year. While the year isn't over, Toyota would have to pull off a radical sales miracle while Honda falls on its face to have the bestselling SUV for 2026. But, if the RAV4 returns to form in 2027, Honda's crown will likely fall. Toyota clocked nearly 480,000 RAV4 sales in 2025, while CR-V might get close to 450,000 this year, one of its best of all time. At least Toyota can claim victory on the hybrid side. Every one of the nearly 40,000 RAV4s it sold last month was either a hybrid or PHEV. Honda saw 53% of CR-V buyers, around 18,500, take home a hybrid model. The main difference is that Toyota moved to a hybrid-only (or PHEV) lineup with this latest generation, while Honda has not. It will be a strange year at Toyota, and probably one it will study for a long time. Until last month, it looked like the Camry would be its bestseller, taking back a title it had held for generations. Now the RAV4 has pulled ahead by around 5,000 units, all but ruling out that possibility as well. Aside from the direct profits from those sales, does capturing the number-one spot really matter beyond bragging rights? Will even more buyers take the CR-V next year if they see Honda putting America's bestselling SUV in ads? Probably not, but Honda probably won't mind the extra attention. title: The Ford Bronco Frostwarden Packs 1200 HP, Courtesy of Its Supercharged 7.3L ‘Megazilla 2.0’ V-8 - Road & Track
content: This search-and-rescue machine, revealed at SEMA, is what happens when Ford throws everything it has at a Bronco. The folks at Ford brought one of the wildest Broncos we’ve ever seen to the 2026 SEMA Show this year. It’s called “Frostwarden” ... and it has 1200 horsepower. How’d Ford extract that much horsepower from a Bronco? Well, it sure doesn’t use any version of the production engines. Instead, Ford put the also-new Megazilla 2.0 crate motor under the hood. This 7.3-liter V-8 is paired here with a 3.0-liter Gen 6 Whipple supercharger; it also has a stronger block, supercharger-specific camshaft, upgraded pistons, larger fuel injectors, and a different belt drive and damper. As a package, Ford is claiming 1200 hp and 1000 pound-feet of torque when run with race fuel. (No, it didn’t quote a pump gas number.) The idea behind the rest of the rig was to put together a package that could be used as an arctic search-and-rescue machine. To that end, it has a custom Bilstein suspension, 74Weld portal gear lifts, upgraded Dana driveline, and 18-inch Weld bead-lock wheels wrapped in 42-inch BFGoodrich tires. It’s absolutely enormous, and gives off the impression that one could drive it anywhere, which is largely the point. This Bronco is festooned with accessories front to back. Rigid lights should help show the way through snowstorms. A spare wheels/tire and pair of toolboxes sit atop the roof. There’s a shovel, recovery rope, fuel jugs, and more. Plus, Ford outfitted the interior with color-matching seats and accents. There’s even a “Megazilla” emblem in the steering wheel rim to make sure you don’t forget this beast has 1200 horsepower ready to unleash. Unfortunately, Ford explicitly says these vehicle “is not available for purchase,” and we suspect something like it never will be from your local Ford dealer. However, it serves as proof that you can shoehorn a 7.3-liter supercharged V-8 under the (admittedly bulged) hood of a Bronco, and what’s not to love about that? California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. (Read more in CalMatters’ voting guide.) Prop 38: Borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research Proposition 38 would create an $8.4 billion bond largely to fund research into fighting cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s, plus other diseases that can be treated through immunotherapies. Half the money would go to a research institute affiliated with the University of California. The other half would be distributed to select public universities and nonprofits. Drugs created through this research would have to be discounted at 20% for Californians and 10% of any revenue from the drugs would go back to the state general fund. Philanthropist and medical inventor Gary Michelson put this measure on the ballot. (Read more in CalMatters’ voting guide.) This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups. (Read more in CalMatters’ voting guide.) Prop 40: Apply one-time tax to billionaires to fund healthcare and education Proposition 40 would require the estimated 200 Californians whose net worth exceeded $1 billion at the start of this year to pay a one-time 5% tax. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the group that put the measure on the ballot, projects that it would raise roughly $100 billion over five years. That money would be earmarked primarily for healthcare, with some reserved for food assistance and education. If propositions 41 or 42 earn more votes than Proposition 40, this measure would be nullified. (Read more in CalMatters’ voting guide.) This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax. (Read more in CalMatters’ voting guide.) Proposition 42 would make it much harder to create a wealth tax in California by prohibiting new taxes on the mere ownership of assets such as investment accounts, business interests and personal property — assets that are typically only taxed when they are sold or generate income. Like Proposition 41, which also attempts to block Proposition 40 (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 42 would nullify Proposition 40 if it receives more votes, even if the billionaire tax also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax. (Read more in CalMatters’ voting guide.) Prop 43: Raise vote threshold for special tax measures This would make it harder to impose or increase local taxes by raising the threshold for local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives to pass from a simple majority to two-thirds. The two-thirds threshold already applies to taxes proposed by local governments but not by individuals. The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot. (Read more in CalMatters’ voting guide.) Prop 44: Require more clinic spending on patient care Proposition 44 would require community clinics that serve low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The measure directs the attorney general to publish guidance on what spending qualifies and allows the state to fine clinics that don’t spend the full 90%. The labor union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put it on the ballot after pushing a similar bill last year that failed. Clinics failed to keep the measure off the ballot with a lawsuit earlier this year. (Read more in CalMatters’ voting guide.) Prop 45: Speed up environmental reviews for housing and infrastructure Proposition 45 would limit reviews under the state’s landmark environmental law, the California Environmental Quality Act. Placed on the ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce, the measure aims to help developers advance projects they designate as “essential” more quickly and easily. It would impose a 365-day limit on environmental reviews for those projects, including infrastructure like roads and bridges, housing, schools, broadband and wildfire mitigation. It would also require courts to rule within 270 days on lawsuits related to the environmental review law. (Read more in CalMatters’ voting guide.) title: WCCUSD's Measure V: Will voters continue to pay parcel tax for libraries, sports and staffing? - Richmondside
content: Independent nonprofit news for Richmond, CA This is a developing story. Check back for live unofficial election results after the polls close at 8 p.m. A parcel tax that helps fund libraries, sports and staffing at west Contra Costa schools is up for renewal. Measure V, which generates about $10 million annually, has been a critical source of funding for local schools. If voters fail to continue the tax, the district says it will either need to find an additional $8 million a year or find things to cut. Since 2004, the tax has been renewed every four to eight years to raise money for sports and school libraries and to hire dozens of staff members, from counselors and speech therapists to custodians and school safety officers. The district is asking the community to renew it for a nine-year period, beginning July 1, 2027 and expiring on June 30, 2036. It needs a two-thirds majority to pass. The rate has remained the same since voters first approved it — 7.2 cents per square foot of total building area — costing an average homeowner about $96 per year, according to WCCUSD. Seniors and disabled property owners are exempt. Get election results for local, regional and statewide races. For more info.: Visit Richmondside’s voter guide or the Contra Costa County elections page. Over the last decade, the bulk of the money (about $3.5 million) has funded school libraries. The next highest spending categories were $1.5 million for afterschool sports programs and $1.3 million for staff including counselors, psychologists and special education aides. WCCUSD spent an average of $950,000 a year of the parcel tax on core academics, including supplementing teacher salaries and buying textbooks or other curriculum. title: Fat Fender Garage Turned a Utilitarian Truck into an 800-HP Ford GT-Inspired Beast for SEMA - Car and Driver
content: This radical truck is based on a 1956 Ford F-100 but swaps in a new chassis, an 800-hp Coyote V-8, and a modernized cabin with leather bucket seats. Ford has produced a diverse array of vehicles in its 123-year history, from workhorses like the bestselling F-series trucks to supercars like the GT supercar. Now, a small outfit seeks to blend the philosophies of those two vehicles. Fat Fender Garage, a restoration shop based in Arizona, has revealed the GT/FX at SEMA, taking the body of a 1956 F-100 truck and giving it performance chops meant to emulate the capabilities of the Ford GT. The GT/FX’s steel body was drastically reshaped by Fat Fender Garage, with a flatter hood and roof and wider front and rear fenders giving it a more aggressive stance. The custom running boards blend neatly into the rear fenders, while a chin splitter up front and a rear diffuser swiped from a Mustang GT350 give the GT/FX a track-ready look. The bed now features distinctive flared edges, and the tailgate drops down with the push of a button. The side-view mirrors are fashioned from carbon fiber, and the gray paint job is completed with a black racing stripe just offset to the left. The only thing left untouched was the grille, maintaining a tie-back to the original F-100. Behind that grille sits a Gen 3 Ford Coyote 5.0-liter V-8 with a 3.0-liter Whipple supercharger strapped on top, pushing out 800 horsepower and 750 pound-feet of torque. The hearty engine is paired with Ford’s 10R80 10-speed automatic transmission, which routes that muscle to HRE wheels wearing Toyo Proxes Sport 2 tires, measuring a beefy 315/35R-20 at the rear. Stopping duties are handled by Wilwood disc brakes with six-piston front calipers and four-piston rear calipers. The cabin features modern-looking bucket seats; a modern screen and buttons are also part of the transformation, but they’re discreetly integrated. Plus, there’s a concealed climate-control system that blows air through a hidden vent, and there’s also interior LED lighting and a modern audio system. The GT/FX showcases the breadth of Fat Fender Garage’s abilities, from paint to interior trim and exhaust setups. The truck even rides on the company’s own FF1 Performance Coilover chassis, which is designed to provide sporty handling despite the vintage truck’s body on top. Between the bodywork, the cabin, the powertrain, and the chassis, Fat Fender Garage went all in on transforming the F-100 from a utilitarian hauler into a sport truck that blends classic styling with modern power. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan. content: After back-to-back defeats on the road against Atletico de Madrid and Como in the competition, our second home fixture is against the Serie A side. title: House v. NCAA Attorneys Seek $18.6M for Year 1 Settlement Work - Sportico.com
content: Attorneys representing the plaintiffs in the House v. NCAA settlement are asking a federal court to approve $18.6 million in fees for having spent more than 3,430 hours of work monitoring and enforcing the landmark college sports agreement during its first year in existence. In a motion filed late last week, class co-counsel Hagens Berman and Winston Taylor (formerly Winston & Strawn) asked U.S. Magistrate Judge Nathanael Cousins to award them $3.81 million for work related to “monitoring and enforcing” the settlement, $14.82 million in incentive fees tied to the college athlete revenue-sharing pool and $200,251.26 in related out-of-pocket expenses. Attorneys Jeffrey Kessler and Steve Berman outlined a number of their accomplishments from June 2025 through June 2026 in overseeing the settlement’s injunctive relief. This included the discovery of more than $88 million not included by schools as part of data they provided to the NCAA’s Membership Financial Reporting System (MFRS). The lawyers credited their auditing work with making an additional $44 million in compensation and benefits available to class members during the current academic year. “The monitoring work itself presents comparable complexity: enforcing a first-of-its-kind settlement governing college-athlete NIL rights, auditing complex financial data, establishing novel arbitration procedures and navigating a rapidly evolving regulatory and legislative landscape,” the attorneys wrote in their motion. They also highlighted their role in monitoring federal legislation, particularly the Protect College Sports Act and their discussions with senators and staff about the House settlement’s structure and objectives. The House defendants previously disclosed to the court that Division I members spent a combined $1.976 billion through the revenue-sharing pool for 2026-27. Class counsel notes this figure exceeded the projection offered by their expert witness by more than $300 million. Under the settlement, class counsel may seek annual payments of up to 1.25% of the amount of money schools spend on athlete revenue-sharing during that period. In their latest petition, however, the attorneys are ultimately seeking a lower rate of 0.75%. Kessler and Berman also noted they are not seeking compensation for nearly $2.73 million in additional billable work they performed over the past year. That work included addressing pending appeals of the final settlement approval and “responding to an enormous volume of inquiries” from class members regarding sale of their claims to third-party claims purchasers. In accompanying declarations, class counsel disclosed hourly billing rates ranging from $2,250 for their firms’ most experienced partners down to $500 for the most junior associate. The requested annual fees would be in addition to the nearly $515 million U.S. District Court Judge Claudia Wilken agreed to award the lawyers in July 2025, following the approval of the $2.78 billion settlement. All of the money, including the backpay damages to class members, will remain in escrow and not be distributed unless or until the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejects petitioners’ challenge to the settlement. The 11 consolidated appeals are scheduled to go before a 9th Circuit hearing on Dec. 7. Two days later, Cousins is set to hold a hearing on class counsel’s latest fee petition. title: Emmett Mosley V Makes Strong Case For Bigger Role in Texas Longhorns Offense - Sports Illustrated
content: Emmett Mosley V has had up-and-down usage in the Texas Longhorns' offense during the 2026 season. Against the Mississippi State Bulldogs, during a 31-3 win in Week 9 at Darrell K Royal-Memorial Stadium, though, Mosley is making a case for more targets on offense. Mosley went for 98 yards on his four catches, one of them a 42-yard touchdown reception where he beat Mississippi State defensive back Dre Riley on a straight go route down the sideline. On the play,  Mosley's burst was off the line of scrimmage was impressive, burning Riley right off the snap. Elsewhere in this game, though, you saw how versatile Mosley can be when allowed to dig into his route tree. Mosley also gained 37 yards on a corner route. He was used on short in routes as well to move the chains. Mosley was everywhere, lining up not in just the slot but also on the boundary. Mosley was split out wide when he scored his first touchdown of the season. Safeties will need to focus extra attention on Mosley's verticality, which should benefit the run and short/intermediate passing games for others. Of course, he may need to be used more in the future like he was against State out of necessity, not just because he showed that he has the skillset to be everywhere in the passing game for Arch Manning. Saturday night was like many other nights on the Forty Acres this season: filled with bad injury news. The receiving corps was hit particularly hard. Cam Coleman exited with injury in the first half before Ryan Wingo suffered an injury of his own later in the game. It's unclear if either will miss time, but it's possible that at least one of them is absent against the Missouri Tigers in Columbia next weekend. This is the meat of the schedule. After Missouri is the LSU Tigers in Death Valley. Get past these two teams, and there are still underperforming historical rivals in trap games: the Arkansas Razorbacks in the home finale in Week 12 and a date with the Texas A&M Aggies in College Station on Black Friday to end the regular season. If Mosley has to be the alpha receiver, he certainly proved he could handle WR-X responsibilities. While he hasn't been the go-to target in red zone situations, perhaps Steve Sarkisian has seen the light after Mosley's breakout against the Bulldogs. It's not an ideal situation, but Texas is uniquely positioned to survive Coleman and/or Wingo being absent for a few weeks with Mosley and emerging true freshman Jermaine Bishop Jr. Mosley has earned the chance to be Manning's new favorite target with injuries hitting the Burnt Orange hard this fall. title: New England Revolution v. Inter Miami: Five Tactical Thoughts - The Blazing Musket
content:

The New England Revolution lost 2-1 to Inter Miami CF on Sunday, meaning second place in the Eastern Conference will, fittingly, come down to Decision Day. The Revs struck in the 59th minute when Daniel Gazdag scored his second in as many games. Miami fought back through Lionel Messi, who assisted German Berterame in the 69th minute, then scored in the 83rd. While a win would've been massive for the Revs, I was encouraged by a lot of their play. With Jack Harrison and Alhassan Yusuf sidelined, the Revs needed someone to lessen the burden on Carles Gil. Peyton Miller has filled that role, collecting five assists in five games. He now has seven goals and nine assists on the season. Against Miami, Miller was relentless in the wide areas, using his speed to get in behind or dribble past opponents. Look here as he immediately gets forward after helping out defensively. He shows his soccer IQ by slowing down, then accelerating, baiting Gonzalo Lujan into an early yellow. Miller kept taking on Lujan, leading to the go-ahead goal. I love his confidence, as the 18-year-old exploded past his defender before laying off a pass. Miller keeps adding new dimensions to his game, making him a more dangerous attacking threat. His speed, timing, and vision (two chances created) were elite on Sunday, but I was most impressed by his ability to beat opponents on the dribble (2/2). "It's very important," Miller said of winning 1v1 battles. "I think that all of that came with the help of Marko [Mitrovic] working with me every single day. The more I'm taking on guys, the more confident I'm getting." I've been slow to form an opinion on Gazdag because it's hard to join a team so late in the season. Obviously a skilled finisher, I've recently noticed his work rate, passing ability, and spatial awareness. Beyond the goal, Gazdag created two chances, had 92% passing accuracy (47/51), and made five defensive contributions. It wasn't a perfect performance (he was 3/13 in duels and 0/6 on dribble attempts), but he put in the effort. Plus, his well-timed pass to Miller should've put the Revs ahead in the first 45. I really respect how open-minded the Revs coaching staff is. Players must learn the system, but coaches must identify how to best integrate each player. I feel like Gazdag is getting more comfortable each week. "Something that we know about Daniel is that Daniel has the capacity to score goals," Mitrovic said. "He has proven in this league that he can [score goals] over and over again. When Daniel joined us, I think for us the biggest challenge was to learn who he is and how we can use him in the best possible way. But also, for Dániel to learn about us. "I think we’re learning. We’re getting better and better. But I still believe that Daniel will need them time. Since Daniel came to the club, we have players that Daniel still hasn’t had one training session [with]. It’s just [him] learning about them, and we’re still learning about Daniel. But the steps forward are there and that’s what is important." What makes me most confident about this team's direction for this year and beyond is that they've established a clear, effective system. The Revs can play in transition, but they're also confident enough to hold possession until a seam opens. Their rotations help with this, as players frequently swap roles and anyone can push forward. If they lose possession, they typically have a committed, high line ready to win it back. The next clip is long, but it has plenty of good, starting with a calm build from the back. Watch the movement as the Revs keep connecting while searching for an opening. Center backs Ethan Kohler and Joshua Wynder are key in creating unpredictability because they can step into the midfield When Miller's pass is picked off, he momentarily pauses before initiating the press. Matt Polster and Carles Gil join in to prevent Miami from getting far, allowing the Revs to go forward again. Gil ultimately takes a shot that forces a strong save, but I am most impressed by the 90 seconds before that because the Revs showed relentlessness and togetherness. The build before Gazdag's goal is similar, with everyone actively wanting the ball. The outside backs are particularly useful, with Will Sands and Ilay Feingold getting into the final third. In fact, Feingold's flick is the final touch before Gazdag's goal. The Revs will always adjust to their opponents, but they also need to forge their own identity. Sunday's game proved how far they've come. "That's probably the biggest step forward for us. Can we be who we are, no matter who we play against? That's what matters to us most," Mitrovic said. "All those games, all those training sessions, we are using them to get the best version of ourselves, having clarity of who we want to be." "All those games help us a lot because [if you] look at the last three games, we had three very unique, different styles of playing where you have to face those teams, and you have to use tools that you have and adapt to teams that have a strong identity on the field. "Philly, Red Bull [New York] their identity. Now, Inter [Miami CF] has so much quality everywhere around the field. And that's where we thrive, is exactly what you're saying. We want to be who we are, and we are ready to live with the outcome as long as we have the right intentions on the field. Whatever the outcome is, we just keep going." While the Revs gave Miami a few chances, Messi unlocked the game, scoring and assisting within 14 minutes. Both moments were hard to defend: the header to Berterame was subtle, and Telasco Segovia helped with the determined march forward. Obviously the Revs will look at what they can do better, but sometimes star players do star player things. "I think when you play against players like [Messi], he’s top-notch; probably the best player in the history of this game," Mitrovic said. "They have those inspirational moments when they can come up. I think the goal that he scored actually was kind of like a little bit, mess around, and he has a high level of execution to execute those things. Players at the highest level are the players that have that inside of them, they can convert those small situations in their favor. I think before that, we had good control of Messi, but one thing with players like Messi is they need that inspirational moment that can change a game in any given situation." Playing against Miami is a difficult task because they have game-changers who can step up at any moment. As such, little moments matter. Such was the case when Brooklyn Raines made a heroic goal-line clearance. Or when Ian Fray's own goal, which would've made it 2-2, was overturned on video review for offside. The Revs lost on Sunday, but they certainly weren't outplayed. Sometimes it comes down to the margins. Share it with friends and help reliable news reach more people.
